rv.q: You would have to have a heart of stone not to find Henry's story deeply moving.
The punch of this heart-soaring production is that it clings onto the light within the darkness – and there's giggles aplenty.
This gives the show an infectious energy of hope and purpose, but at the expense of jeopardy and enduring discomfort.
It is a lovable tearjerker nonetheless with a disarming sweetness and bearing all the signs of being an immense crowd-pleaser.
If the show doesn’t feel completely achieved, it breaks new ground and takes its audience on an exceptional journey.
There’s plenty to admire about this show, from its inclusive spirit to its harnessing of big emotions, but it lacks detail and nuance: those crucial little things.
It’s just a pity that this story doesn’t come fully alive.
If you’re allergic to musical theatre earnestness, new British musical The Little Big Things will have you reaching for the epi pen.
Because this show, this brilliant show, grabs you, grips you and stubbornly and resolutely refuses to let you go.
This triumphant new musical, based on artist Henry Fraser’s authentically inspirational memoir of the same name, is a real workout for the emotions.
This is a production you won’t forget in a hurry — and for all the right reasons.
Director Luke Sheppard directs The Little Big Things as an ensemble work full of strong characterisations, and it wins its audience over with its energy and a compassion that never becomes mawkish.
The Little Big Things is by no means perfect. There are missed opportunities for musical numbers... but these are moot points against such a welcome wave of positivity.
Moments of blame and doubt bring needed complexity to a piece that feels a few songwriting rewrites short of its full potential.
On the whole, it makes for a diverting night out.
Played by the dazzling Amy Trigg, she’s the best thing in this bland piece of community theatre.
Perfect feels like the most fitting word to describe this show as everything about it is absolutely faultless.
This new British musical is the best thing to happen to London theatre in years.
It’s a true story (book by Joe White) about the transformative power of family, about taking the positive from disaster and running with it.
The Little Big Things is a MOMENTOUS success for London’s newest build theatre in 50 years.
The problem, however, lies in the extent to which The Little Big Things indulges itself in self-pity, despair and tragedy.

We found The Little Big Things very moving, had tears in our eyes almost throughout knowing the inevitable accident to come but also that a different kind of triumph is required to meet the challenge set.

cn.t: Critics praise this big-hearted musical about Henry Fraser's life-changing accident as emotionally powerful and crowd-pleasing, though some find it overly earnest. Strong performances and accessible storytelling win acclaim despite occasional schmaltz.
